title: SQLite vs PostgreSQL
subtitle: Dialect differences, Python integration, and choosing the right database
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: SQL is a standard but every database has different data types, functions, and features. What works in SQLite may not work in PostgreSQL. Understanding the differences prevents surprises when moving to production.
whyItExists.solution: Learn the key differences between SQLite (embedded, file-based, zero-config) and PostgreSQL (client-server, production-grade, feature-rich). Understand how to connect and query both from Python.
whyItExists.whenToUse: SQLite: development, local apps, mobile, embedded. PostgreSQL: production web apps, concurrent users, complex queries, JSON, full-text search, large data.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Don't use SQLite for high-concurrency web apps — it has a single writer. Don't use PostgreSQL when you need a zero-config file-based database — SQLite is simpler.

explainModes.beginner: SQLite is like a spreadsheet file — the whole database lives in one .db file, no server needed. PostgreSQL is a full server — it runs as a background process, handles many users at once, and is used in real web applications. Both speak SQL, but with small differences.
explainModes.simple: SQLite: file-based, zero config, great for dev/mobile. PostgreSQL: server-based, handles concurrent users, production-grade. Key differences: data types (INTEGER/REAL/TEXT vs INT/DECIMAL/VARCHAR), booleans (0/1 vs TRUE/FALSE), date functions (DATE('now') vs NOW()), AUTOINCREMENT vs SERIAL/IDENTITY. Python: sqlite3 (stdlib) vs psycopg2/asyncpg. Connection strings. Parameterized queries (? vs %s).
explainModes.standard: SQLite dynamic typing: any value can go in any column. PostgreSQL strict typing: 'hello' in an INTEGER column is an error. SQLite concurrency: WAL mode allows one writer + concurrent readers; still single-writer. PostgreSQL: full MVCC, many concurrent writers. SQLite foreign keys: off by default (PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON). PostgreSQL: on by default. SQLite: no user/role system. PostgreSQL: full role-based access control. Migration path: SQLite for prototyping, PostgreSQL for production with minimal query changes.
explainModes.technical: Python sqlite3: standard library, synchronous, .db file. Parameterized: cursor.execute('SELECT * FROM t WHERE id=?', (id,)). Python psycopg2: external package, synchronous, DSN connection string. Parameterized: cursor.execute('SELECT * FROM t WHERE id=%s', (id,)). asyncpg: async PostgreSQL driver. SQLAlchemy ORM: abstracts both databases — switch by changing the connection string. Alembic: migration tool for SQLAlchemy. psycopg3 (psycopg): new async-first driver.
explainModes.deepDive: SQLite use cases in production: local-first apps (synced later), mobile apps, embedded systems, CLI tools, test fixtures. Turso (libSQL) extends SQLite for multi-tenant cloud. PostgreSQL extensions: pg_vector for AI embeddings, pg_trgm for fuzzy search, PostGIS for geospatial, TimescaleDB for time-series. Connection pooling: PgBouncer sits between app and PostgreSQL, reusing connections. PostgreSQL LISTEN/NOTIFY: real-time pub-sub over the database connection. Logical replication for read replicas and CDC (Change Data Capture).

content.code:
-- ─────────────────────────────────────────
-- SQLite                  PostgreSQL
-- ─────────────────────────────────────────

-- AUTO-INCREMENT
-- SQLite:      INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT
-- PostgreSQL:  id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY
--              id INTEGER GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY

-- CURRENT TIMESTAMP
-- SQLite:      DATETIME('now'), DATE('now')
-- PostgreSQL:  NOW(), CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, CURRENT_DATE

-- BOOLEANS (SQLite has no BOOLEAN type)
-- SQLite:      INTEGER (0 = false, 1 = true)
-- PostgreSQL:  BOOLEAN (TRUE/FALSE)

-- STRING functions
-- SQLite:      || for concatenation, instr(), substr()
-- PostgreSQL:  || or CONCAT(), position(), substring()

-- JSON
-- SQLite:      json() (basic), json_extract()
-- PostgreSQL:  JSON, JSONB (binary, indexed), -> and ->> operators

-- FULL TEXT SEARCH
-- SQLite:      FTS5 extension
-- PostgreSQL:  tsvector, tsquery, @@ operator, GIN indexes

-- ENABLE FOREIGN KEYS (SQLite only)
PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;

# ── SQLite (stdlib, no install needed) ──
import sqlite3

# Connect to a file (creates it if it doesn't exist)
conn = sqlite3.connect('mydb.db')
conn.row_factory = sqlite3.Row  # rows as dict-like objects

# Enable foreign keys
conn.execute('PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON')

cur = conn.cursor()

# Parameterized query — use ? placeholders
cur.execute('SELECT * FROM users WHERE city = ?', ('Delhi',))
for row in cur.fetchall():
    print(row['name'], row['email'])

# Insert with transaction
with conn:  # auto-commits or rolls back on exception
    conn.execute(
        'INSERT INTO users (name, email, city, joined_at) VALUES (?,?,?,?)',
        ('New User', 'new@example.com', 'Pune', '2024-07-01')
    )
    row_id = conn.execute('SELECT last_insert_rowid()').fetchone()[0]
    print('Inserted ID:', row_id)

conn.close()

# ── PostgreSQL (install: pip install psycopg2-binary) ──
import psycopg2
from psycopg2.extras import RealDictCursor

# Connection string
conn = psycopg2.connect(
    host='localhost',
    port=5432,
    dbname='mydb',
    user='postgres',
    password='secret'
    # or: dsn='postgresql://postgres:secret@localhost:5432/mydb'
)
conn.autocommit = False  # explicit transactions

# Use %s placeholders (not ?) for PostgreSQL
with conn.cursor(cursor_factory=RealDictCursor) as cur:
    cur.execute('SELECT * FROM users WHERE city = %s', ('Delhi',))
    for row in cur.fetchall():
        print(row['name'], row['email'])

# Commit / rollback
try:
    with conn.cursor() as cur:
        cur.execute(
            'INSERT INTO users (name, email, city) VALUES (%s, %s, %s) RETURNING id',
            ('New User', 'new@example.com', 'Pune')
        )
        new_id = cur.fetchone()[0]
    conn.commit()
except Exception:
    conn.rollback()
    raise
finally:
    conn.close()

# pip install sqlalchemy
from sqlalchemy import create_engine, text

# SQLite
engine = create_engine('sqlite:///mydb.db')

# PostgreSQL
# engine = create_engine('postgresql+psycopg2://user:pass@localhost/mydb')

# Same code works for both!
with engine.connect() as conn:
    result = conn.execute(text('SELECT * FROM users WHERE city = :city'),
                          {'city': 'Delhi'})
    for row in result:
        print(row.name, row.email)

questions.question: Which parameter placeholder do you use in Python's psycopg2 for PostgreSQL?
questions.explanation: psycopg2 uses %s as the parameterized placeholder: cursor.execute('SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = %s', (user_id,)). SQLite's sqlite3 uses ?. Both drivers handle escaping for you — never use string formatting (f-strings or %) to build SQL queries with user input, as that causes SQL injection.

faq.q: When should I use SQLite vs PostgreSQL?
faq.a: SQLite: local/desktop apps, CLI tools, development databases, mobile apps, single-user or low-concurrency scenarios. Its main limit is single-writer — only one INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE at a time. PostgreSQL: any web application with concurrent users, when you need JSON, full-text search, robust role-based access, logical replication, or extension ecosystem. Start with SQLite for development — its schema is valid PostgreSQL SQL with minor adjustments.

faq.q: How do I migrate from SQLite to PostgreSQL?
faq.a: The SQL is largely compatible with small changes: AUTOINCREMENT → SERIAL or GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY, DATE('now') → NOW(), INTEGER boolean columns → BOOLEAN TRUE/FALSE. Use SQLAlchemy with Alembic migrations to manage schema changes across both databases. The pgloader tool can migrate SQLite data directly to PostgreSQL.
